findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. They can describe the product after one paragraph.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page says why a page at Athena's address is about a different project, firstmate: the study is a demonstration. Without that sentence a newcomer would be confused by the title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work".
findings.source: header lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it..."

findings.text: A link near the top jumps to concrete next steps: prerequisites (git 2.40+, a C linker, curl, Claude Code or npm), `git clone`, `./setup.sh`, and a first command, `athena ask "add a changelog"`. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and heading "Next steps"

findings.text: Athena is described as written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not list a Rust toolchain, and the page does not say whether setup.sh installs one. A newcomer may not know if they need cargo first.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link appears in the introduction but is not explained. A newcomer does not know who "the owner" is or why proposals would wait for them, so it reads as a distraction.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine breakdown of firstmate, with codes such as t1–t12, exit statuses and ids like ra1. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena will likely skim it. It shows the claim-tracing well but is hard going as a first impression.
findings.source: headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (cards t1–t12, "exit 75", "places-held")

findings.text: The list of states shows only names and tags, with no descriptions. A reader has to go to the Glossary to learn what "close-pending" or "ready" means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "Read each line as the state's name, its kind, and the claims that support it."

findings.text: The early definitions use terms before defining them: green is defined by red, which comes next, and PR is first spelled out at the end of the page. This is minor, but it trips a first-time reader.
findings.source: Words used first: "green — A PR that is not red" (listed before "red"; "PR" is defined only in the Glossary)

findings.text: The closing sections use Athena's internal wording ("the job", "recorded boundary", a studies/ folder in an unnamed repository) that a newcomer cannot decode.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate"; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"
